lesson.title: 68, 95, 99.7: The Numbers Every Bell Curve Obeys
lesson.summary: The 68-95-99.7 rule gives the exact percentages of data in a normal distribution falling within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean, providing a fast way to estimate probabilities and identify unusual values.
lesson.body:
The empirical rule becomes a genuinely usable tool once its percentages are stated precisely. For any approximately normal distribution, about 68 percent of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95 percent fall within two standard deviations, and about 99.7 percent, essentially almost all of the data, fall within three standard deviations. These three figures, 68, 95, and 99.7, give the rule its common shorthand name, and they hold regardless of what the mean and standard deviation actually are, as long as the underlying distribution is close to normal.

Because the normal curve is symmetric, each of these percentages splits evenly on both sides of the mean. If 68 percent of the data lies within one standard deviation, then the remaining 32 percent lies outside that range, split into 16 percent in the lower tail and 16 percent in the upper tail. Likewise, if 95 percent lies within two standard deviations, 5 percent lies outside, split into 2.5 percent in each tail, and if 99.7 percent lies within three standard deviations, only 0.3 percent lies outside, split into 0.15 percent in each tail. This tail-splitting trick, dividing the leftover percentage by two, is what turns the rule from a description of the middle of the data into a tool for finding probabilities in one specific tail.

Consider adult male height, approximately normal with a mean of 70 inches and a standard deviation of 3 inches. One standard deviation below and above the mean gives 70 minus 3, or 67 inches, and 70 plus 3, or 73 inches, so about 68 percent of men are between 67 and 73 inches tall. Two standard deviations gives 70 minus 6, or 64 inches, and 70 plus 6, or 76 inches, so about 95 percent of men are between 64 and 76 inches tall. Three standard deviations gives 70 minus 9, or 61 inches, and 70 plus 9, or 79 inches, so about 99.7 percent of men fall between 61 and 79 inches, leaving only about 0.3 percent, roughly 3 in 1000, either shorter than 61 inches or taller than 79 inches.

That same height example shows the rule's tail-splitting power directly. Since 95 percent of men fall between 64 and 76 inches, the remaining 5 percent is split evenly between the two tails, giving 2.5 percent of men taller than 76 inches and, by the same logic, 2.5 percent shorter than 64 inches. Estimating that a man over 6 feet 4 inches, which is 76 inches, is among roughly the tallest 2.5 percent of the adult male population took nothing more than knowing the mean, the standard deviation, and this rule, no calculator or table required.

The 68-95-99.7 rule is fast, but it only works exactly at whole numbers of standard deviations: one, two, or three. A height of 74 inches, sitting between one and two standard deviations above the mean, cannot be pinned down with this rule alone. Answering questions at values in between requires the more general tool built next, the standard normal curve, which extends this same idea to any distance from the mean, not just whole standard deviations.
